events.excerpt: Summary This proposal introduces post-quantum signature aggregation with leanVM in shadow mode . BLS remains the only authority for aggregates: consensus validity depends on BLS alone, exactly as today. leanVM aggregates and proofs are produced and verified alongside BLS, but their results have no effect on consensus. They are only measured, compared, and reported. When PQ/AI day arrives, an emergency hard fork simply retires BLS and enables leanVM in full. By “PQ/AI day” we mean the point at which quantum computers, or AI-assisted cryptanalysis, make BLS unsafe to rely on. Motivation Ethereum has to be ready for post-quantum signatures well before BLS is actually broken. Waiting until the last moment would mean deploying new, complex code to mainnet in a hurry. Giving leanVM authority early has its own risk: leanVM is new code that hasn’t been tested in production. However carefully it is built and audited, we can’t rule out a soundness bug that accepts an invalid proof, or a liveness bug that rejects a valid one. The main benefit of shadow mode is that Ethereum isn’t put at risk from a leanVM bug before PQ/AI day arrives. Because leanVM has no authority, a leanVM bug can’t break Ethereum’s security or halt the chain. At the same time, leanVM runs on mainnet under real load, so by the time it needs authority it is battle-tested code rather than something enabled in a hurry. There are updates on the progress of the Sylve project, which is an attempt to bring a smooth polished GUI for managing FreeBSD virtualization hosts – something akin to Proxmox for FreeBSD. We mentioned this when we looked at the new Daemonarchy project last month. Another covers the new AppJail effort – a containerized app distribution system for FreeBSD, including for GUI apps, which aims for something broadly comparable to Snap, Flatpak and AppImage on Linux. events.excerpt: This release removes Bitswap in favour of shrex, adds JWT token revocation, and ships a set of security and stability fixes. It is compatible with celestia-app v10 and with v0.34.x nodes on the network, so no coordinated upgrade is needed. It is recommended to upgrade. Action Recommended: run config-update This release removes the unused Share.UseShareExchange , Share.UseBitswap and Share.BlockStoreCacheSize keys from the config. Nodes start without this step and ignore the old keys. To remove them from your config.toml , stop the node, upgrade the binary and, before starting the node , run: celestia bridge config-update celestia light config-update Your custom values for the other fields are kept. Review your config.toml afterwards to confirm. Breaking changes & upgrade notes Bitswap removed: shrex is now the only share exchange protocol ( #5378 ). v0.35.0 nodes keep working with v0.34.x peers, which already used shrex first and Bitswap only as a fallback. The Share.UseShareExchange , Share.UseBitswap and Share.BlockStoreCacheSize config options are removed. Existing config files still load and the keys are ignored. Nodes that had disabled shrex now use it. On first start, light nodes delete the samples that the Bitswap client left in the datastore. This runs once. The cel-shed shwap command is removed. Go API changes: The share/shwap/p2p/bitswap package is removed. rpc.NewServer now takes an *authtoken.Verifier instead of a jwt.Verifier . Custom implementations of nodebuilder/node.Module must also implement AuthRevoke ( #5364 ). Go version: source builds now require Go 1.

events.excerpt: Advocates for cloud-native software have long argued that their approach to development makes applications portable across different Kubernetes environments. But VMware argues that’s not happening across hybrid clouds, and has taken the lead in an effort to improve matters. That effort, the new Workload Conformance Working Group in the Kubernetes community, aims to establish a shared standard for how workloads run on Kubernetes. The group’s web page points out, “Certified Kubernetes tests the cluster, and Kubernetes AI Conformance tests whether a cluster can run AI and ML workloads. Nothing comparable exists for the workloads themselves, so cluster operators still check each application by hand before routine maintenance or a Kubernetes upgrade. Every cluster operator ends up repeating the same assessment, and application maintainers get the same questions from each environment they support,” the group asserts. The proposed solution? “A common specification with repeatable tests would give both groups the same baseline to start from.” Prashanth Shenoy, VP of product marketing in Broadcom's VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) division, told The Register that standard is needed in part because applications packaged to run in public clouds don’t always run well in hybrid clouds. events.excerpt: AMD's upcoming Verano processors aren't like any Epyc CPUs we've seen before. Rather than general-purpose workloads, Verano is designed specifically to power AMD's next generation of GPU servers. In an interview with The Register during a press event in Las Vegas last week, Madhu Rangarajan, corporate VP of AMD's compute and enterprise AI products business, described Verano as being the first step towards building something that more closely resembles Nvidia's Vera Rubin superchips. "Verano is really designed for an integrated CPU+GPU rack scale solution," he said. "From that perspective, I wouldn't say the CPU is a competitor to Vera. In a head note, I'd say the Verano+GPU solution is a competitor to Vera+Rubin." For reference, Vera Rubin and the GB200 and GB300 that came before it aren't your typical server platforms. Instead they're more like an enormous single-board computer combining CPUs and GPUs into a tightly-integrated package. Each of Nvidia's superchips joins a single 88-core Vera CPU and 1.5 TB of LPDDR5X memory to a pair of Rubin GPUs via Nvidia's speedy NVLink-C2C interconnect. Rangarajan tells us Verano will be the host CPU for a similar class of product using AMD GPUs, and much like Nvidia's superchips, the CPU will also use notebook memory rather than conventional RDIMMS. However, unlike Vera, which is also being deployed as a standalone CPU in storage servers and agent sandboxes, Verano has a singular purpose: keeping its GPUs fed. (We assume they'll be MI500X GPUs.)
